newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: 150,000 protest in Belgrade over poll annulment.
newsitem.headline: 150,000 protest in Belgrade over poll annulment.

text.p: An estimated 150,000 Serbians demonstrated in Belgrade on Monday, some pelting state media offices with eggs, and their leaders pledged to force President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialists to accept election results.

The United States condemned the annulment of the municipal election results, which had showed victories for the anti-Milosevic Zajedno (Together) coalition, and European Union officials and diplomats from 13 Western embassies talked with Zajedno leaders.
Zoran Djindjic, a leader of Zajedno which had claimed victory in local elections eight days ago, told a huge rally in Belgrade they were at the forefront of a revolution.
"This is no longer an election rally or a protest rally. This is a democratic revolution that Serbia has been waiting 50 years for," he said.
In response, the massive crowd chanted "Serbia has risen, Serbia has risen".

Some in a crowd estimated by police at 150,000 hurled eggs at the state-controlled Radio and Television building and the offices of the Politika newspaper, targetting two of President Milosevic's key instruments of power.
The peaceful protesters jeered at the buildings and chanted anti-communist slogans such as "Red Gang" and "Out, out".
"These are not elections between parties," declared one speaker. "These are elections between democracy and darkness."
Later Djindjic told Reuters the demonstration was a massive expression of anger that Milosevic could not ignore.

"Milosevic is a coward. He dares not appear, pretends not to know," the opposition leader said. "In the end, we will call the people to resort to other methods, to strikes in factories and schools. I think everything is going according to plan."
Opposition and student activists said more demonstrations would take place on Tuesday, focusing on the parliament.

After polling eight days ago, the ruling Socialist party at first conceded they had lost councils in major towns across Serbia, including Belgrade, but electoral commissions later annulled the results in almost all the districts Zajedno won.

Monday's protest came a day after the state-controlled electoral commission in Belgrade took back 33 local council seats won by Zajedno, citing unspecified irregularities, and called for a third round of voting on Wednesday.
The state news agency Tanjug declared that a campaign blackout began at midnight on Sunday, in a tactic analysts say was designed to stifle the protests ahead of the polls.
Zajedno has urged a boycott of the third round in the capital and other key towns where they say they were cheated of legal victories.
European Union officials and diplomats from 13 Western embassies talked with Zajedno leaders after a meeting with the Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic over the weekend.
Although diplomatic sources confirmed that the ambassadors discussed the growing crisis, they maintained silence over the diplomats' message.
But a U.S. State Department spokesman stepped up Western pressure on Belgrade, condemning the Socialists' tactics.

Spokesman Glyn Davies told a news conference in Washington the annulment was "totally unacceptable" and said: "Such a step undermines the election process and invalidates Serbia's claim to be a state evolving towards democracy."
Davies' comment was the strongest Western reaction to the crisis so far. Most governments have offered muted statements of concern over possible election fraud.

The United States and European powers once accused Milosevic of igniting war in the former Yugoslavia. They now view him as a guarantor of Balkan peace after he signed the Dayton treaty for Bosnia last year and may wish to avoid open confrontation.
But Western states still have indirect weapons.

These include adding respect for democracy to existing conditions -- such as a peaceful solution to an ethnic dispute in Kosovo and compliance with the Bosnia peace process -- as the price for normalising international relations with Yugoslavia.
